title: Descriptive Writing
description: Build vivid, controlled descriptions using sensory detail, precise word choice, atmosphere and showing-not-telling, and shape them into strong openings for narrative tasks.

notes.heading: What is Descriptive Writing?
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Descriptive writing uses carefully chosen language to create a vivid picture of a person, place, object or moment in the reader's mind.

🔑 Key Concept
Good description is selection, not inventory. A strong writer:
• Chooses a few significant details rather than listing everything
• Gives every detail a job — building atmosphere, revealing character or supporting a mood
• Zooms in on what is unusual, telling or surprising

💡 Worked Example
Weak: 'The room was old and messy.'
Stronger: 'Dust furred the windowsill; a tower of yellowed newspapers leant against the door.'
The second version selects two precise details that imply age and neglect without naming them.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Describe what matters, not everything in sight.
• Specific details beat general labels ('old', 'nice', 'scary').
• Description often works best when it also advances mood or story.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing a list of everything visible in a scene. Readers remember two sharp details, not twenty flat ones.

notes.heading: Sensory Detail Beyond Sight
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Sensory detail is language that appeals to the five senses — sight, sound, smell, touch and taste. Most weak descriptions rely on sight alone.

🔑 Key Concept
• Sound — humming fridges, distant sirens, the tick of a clock in a silent room.
• Smell — strongly linked to memory; one smell can place a reader instantly.
• Touch — textures, temperature, weight: grit, damp, a draught on the neck.
• Taste — useful in food scenes but also for air that 'tastes' of salt or smoke.

💡 Worked Example
Instead of 'The market was busy', try: 'Fishmongers shouted prices over the slap of hoses on stone, and the air hung thick with salt and crushed ice.'

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Aim to use at least three different senses in any full description.
• Sound and smell are the most underused — and often the most evocative.
• Sensory details should still be selected, not piled up.

✅ Check
Cover the visual details in your paragraph. Does anything remain? If not, add sound, smell or touch.

notes.heading: Precise Verbs and Modifiers
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A precise verb names an exact action; a modifier (adjective or adverb) narrows or sharpens a noun or verb. Precision means choosing the single word that does the most work.

🔑 Key Concept
• Upgrade flat verbs: 'walked' → 'trudged', 'strode', 'crept', 'shuffled' — each carries a different mood.
• Cut empty modifiers: 'very big' → 'vast'; 'really scared' → 'terrified'.
• Keep modifiers that add new information, delete ones that merely repeat ('the wet rain').

💡 Worked Example
'The boy went through the door quickly because he was scared' → 'The boy bolted through the door.' One precise verb replaces five words and shows the fear.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• A strong verb often removes the need for an adverb.
• Adjectives earn their place when they add information the noun cannot.
• Read your work aloud and underline every 'very' — replace or delete most of them.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Stacking adjectives ('the big, dark, old, scary house'). Two well-chosen details are stronger than four vague ones.

notes.heading: Showing vs Telling
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Telling states an emotion or quality directly ('She was nervous'). Showing presents the outward evidence — actions, gestures, dialogue, physical detail — and lets the reader draw the conclusion.

🔑 Key Concept
• Replace emotion labels with observable behaviour.
• Use the body: hands, breath, eyes, posture.
• Let objects and setting carry feeling: a chair pushed back too fast, a cup refilled but never sipped.

💡 Worked Example
Telling: 'Marcus was nervous about the results.'
Showing: 'Marcus folded the envelope in half, then quarters, then flattened it smooth again on the desk.'

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Showing creates trust: readers enjoy working out how a character feels.
• Telling is not banned — use it for quick, unimportant information.
• Show the emotions that matter; tell the transitions that do not.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Showing and then telling anyway: 'Her hands trembled. She was terrified.' Trust the detail — delete the label.

notes.heading: Atmosphere and Mood
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Atmosphere is the emotional feeling of a place or scene as created by the writer; mood is the feeling the reader experiences in response. Writers build both through setting, weather, light, colour and sound.

🔑 Key Concept
• Pathetic fallacy — the environment mirrors or sets emotion (a storm for conflict, fog for uncertainty).
• Light and colour — long shadows, sodium-orange streetlights, a grey flat sky.
• Sound — or its absence: silence can be more unsettling than noise.
• Small wrongness — one detail out of place (an open window in winter) creates unease.

💡 Worked Example
To build tension before a character enters a house: 'The gate hung open. Somewhere inside, a radio murmured to no one, and every curtain on the street was drawn except his.'

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Decide the atmosphere first, then select details that serve it.
• Consistency matters — a cheerful detail can deflate a tense scene.
• Atmosphere should shift with the story; static mood becomes monotonous.

✅ Check
Name the atmosphere of your scene in one word. Can you point to three details that create it?

notes.heading: Structuring a Description
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Structure is the order in which you reveal details. A description needs a deliberate path, just like a camera movement in film.

🔑 Key Concept
Common structures include:
• Zoom out → in — start with the wide scene, then narrow to one significant detail.
• Zoom in → out — open on a striking small detail, then reveal the wider scene around it.
• Movement through space — follow a character walking, letting the scene unfold in the order they encounter it.
• Time shift — describe the same place at two different times to show change.

💡 Worked Example
Market scene (zoom in): wide shot of the crowd and stalls → one stall's pyramids of fruit → a single bruised plum rolling off the edge into the gutter.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Link details with movement or logic, not 'and then... and then'.
• End on a resonant detail that echoes the mood — your last image lingers.
• Paragraph breaks can mark a change of focus, distance or time.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Jumping randomly between details with no guiding path, so the reader cannot build a picture.

notes.heading: Figurative Language & Descriptive Openings
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Figurative language — simile, metaphor, personification — describes one thing in terms of another. It earns its place when it is fresh, apt and consistent with the mood.

🔑 Key Concept
• A good image surprises but still fits: 'The cold snapped at her fingers' suits a harsh scene; it would jar in a gentle one.
• Avoid clichés ('as white as snow', 'a blanket of stars') — they are invisible to readers.
• One or two strong images per paragraph beat five competing ones.

💡 Worked Example
Descriptive opening for a narrative task: 'The harbour smelled of rust and low tide. Beyond the sea wall, the ferry exhaled black smoke and waited, and Tom counted his money for the third time.' — setting, atmosphere and a hint of conflict in two sentences.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Open narrative tasks inside the scene, not with 'It was a sunny day'.
• Hint at a problem or question early — description should promise story.
• Match your images to the atmosphere you chose.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Mixing clashing images ('the waves roared like lions, gentle as a lullaby, knives of white foam') — pick one controlling image and stay with it.

flashcards.definition: Writing that uses detailed, sensory language to create a vivid picture of a person, place, object or moment.
flashcards.example: A paragraph that makes the reader feel the chill and echo of an empty station at midnight.

flashcards.definition: Language that appeals to the five senses — sight, sound, smell, touch and taste.
flashcards.example: 'The chips hissed in the fryer and the air tasted of vinegar' uses sound, smell and taste.

flashcards.definition: A verb that names an exact action, carrying mood and meaning without needing extra words.
flashcards.example: 'Trudged' is more precise than 'walked slowly and unhappily'.

flashcards.definition: An adjective or adverb that narrows or sharpens the meaning of a noun or verb.
flashcards.example: In 'a hairline crack', the modifier 'hairline' tells us exactly what kind of crack.

flashcards.definition: Presenting the outward evidence of an emotion or quality — action, gesture, detail — instead of naming it directly.
flashcards.example: Instead of 'she was angry': 'She set the mug down harder than she meant to.'

flashcards.definition: The emotional feeling of a place or scene, created through setting, weather, light, colour and sound.
flashcards.example: Drawn curtains, a murmuring radio and an open gate create an uneasy atmosphere.

flashcards.definition: The feeling experienced by the reader in response to the writer's choices.
flashcards.example: A scene with thick fog and muffled footsteps puts the reader in a tense, watchful mood.

flashcards.definition: Using weather or the natural environment to mirror or set a character's emotions.
flashcards.example: A thunderstorm breaking during an argument reflects the characters' fury.

flashcards.definition: Ordering a description like a camera movement — from wide scene to small detail, or the reverse.
flashcards.example: City skyline → one street → a single lit window where someone waits.

flashcards.definition: A comparison between two things using 'like' or 'as'.
flashcards.example: 'The frost lay like salt on the pavement.'

flashcards.definition: Describing one thing as if it were another, without using 'like' or 'as'.
flashcards.example: 'The classroom was a furnace by third period.'

flashcards.definition: Giving human qualities or actions to non-human things.
flashcards.example: 'The wind nagged at the loose shutter all night.'

questions.stem: Descriptive writing should aim to appeal to how many of the reader's senses?
choices: Only sight — it is about creating a picture
Two: sight and sound
All five, though not necessarily in every paragraph
None — description is about facts
questions.explanation: Strong description draws on all five senses across a piece. Sound, smell and touch are often the most evocative because writers overuse sight.

questions.stem: What does the advice 'show, don't tell' mean?
choices: Never state anything directly in your writing
Present the evidence of an emotion through action and detail rather than naming it
Use pictures instead of words where possible
Tell the reader the plot but not the setting
questions.explanation: Showing means replacing labels like 'she was scared' with observable detail — trembling hands, held breath — so readers draw the conclusion themselves.

questions.stem: Which is the most precise replacement for 'walked' in 'The exhausted hiker walked up the hill'?
choices: Went
Moved
Trudged
Travelled
questions.explanation: 'Trudged' means walking slowly and heavily with effort, so it carries the exhaustion in a single word. 'Went' and 'moved' are even flatter than 'walked'.

questions.stem: A simile compares two things using which words?
choices: 'Like' or 'as'
'Is' or 'was'
'And' or 'but'
'Because' or 'so'
questions.explanation: A simile makes a comparison explicit with 'like' or 'as' ('the frost lay like salt'). A metaphor states that one thing is another instead.

choices: The weather forecast for the setting
The emotional feeling of a place or scene created by the writer's details
The list of characters present in the scene
The grammatical tense of the description
questions.explanation: Atmosphere is the emotional charge of a scene — tense, peaceful, eerie — built through choices about light, weather, sound and detail.

questions.stem: Which sentence best SHOWS that Amara is nervous rather than telling us?
choices: Amara was very nervous about the audition.
Amara felt extremely anxious and worried.
Amara read her sheet music until the words blurred, then realised she had been humming the same bar for a minute.
Amara, a nervous person by nature, entered the hall.
questions.explanation: The blurred music and repeated humming are observable behaviours that reveal nerves without naming them. The other options simply label the emotion.

questions.stem: In the 'zoom' structure for a description, 'zooming in' means:
choices: Writing faster and faster
Moving from a wide view of the scene towards one small, significant detail
Adding more adjectives to every noun
Describing everything at the same level of detail
questions.explanation: Zooming in mirrors a camera: start wide so the reader is oriented, then narrow to the detail that matters most, giving the description direction and focus.

questions.stem: 'Rain hammered the windows as the two brothers argued over the will.' This is an example of:
choices: Pathetic fallacy — the storm mirrors the conflict
A mixed metaphor
An informal register
A narrative flashback
questions.explanation: The violent weather echoes the characters' fury, which is exactly how pathetic fallacy works: the environment is used to mirror emotion.

questions.stem: Why are sound and smell often more effective than visual detail in a description?
choices: They are easier to spell
They are underused, so they feel fresh, and smell in particular triggers memory and immersion
Examiners are required to give them more marks
They always make writing longer
questions.explanation: Most writers default to sight, so sound and smell surprise the reader; smell is also strongly linked to memory, which makes scenes feel immediate and real.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest opening line for a narrative task titled 'The Wait'?
choices: It was a normal Tuesday and the weather was quite nice.
In this story I am going to describe a waiting room.
The clock in the corridor had stopped at eleven minutes past four, and nobody had fixed it, and nobody would look at it.
Have you ever wondered what waiting feels like?
questions.explanation: It drops the reader into a specific scene with a wrong, unsettling detail that hints at tension — a strong opening promises story. The others are flat, meta or generic.

questions.stem: 'The cold snapped at her fingers as she fumbled for the keys.' What technique does 'snapped' create here?
choices: Simile — the cold is compared to an animal
Personification — the cold is given a hostile, animal-like action
Onomatopoeia — the word copies a sound
Hyperbole — the cold is exaggerated for humour
questions.explanation: 'Snapped' gives the cold a deliberate, aggressive action as if it were a living attacker, which is personification. There is no 'like' or 'as', so it is not a simile.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses figurative language most effectively for a tense scene?
choices: The fog was as thick as pea soup and the night was as black as coal.
The fog unspooled between the streetlights, erasing the end of the road.
The fog was a lion, a blanket, a wall of knives, and it roared gently.
The fog was very thick and it was hard to see far ahead of us.
questions.explanation: One fresh, controlled image ('unspooled', 'erasing') builds unease. Option A uses clichés, C mixes clashing images, and D has no figurative language at all.

questions.stem: Why can packing every sentence with metaphors and similes weaken a description?
choices: Figurative language is against the rules of descriptive writing
The images compete for attention, the mood blurs, and individual details lose impact
Readers prefer descriptions with no adjectives
Metaphors are only allowed in poetry
questions.explanation: Figurative language works by standing out. When every sentence strains for effect, nothing stands out, and competing images make the scene harder to picture.

questions.stem: A writer wants to describe a busy market as a character walks from one end to the other. Which structure fits the task best?
choices: Describe every stall alphabetically by what it sells
Movement through space — reveal details in the order the character encounters them
Start with the history of the market town
List all the smells first, then all the sounds, then all the sights
questions.explanation: Following the character's walk gives the description a natural path and lets the scene unfold for the reader as it unfolds for the character. The other orders feel arbitrary.

questions.stem: 'The house was old. The house was scary. We went into the house slowly.' Which revision shows the strongest descriptive control?
choices: The house was very old, very scary and we very slowly went into it.
The old, scary, dark, big, empty house was entered by us slowly.
Paint hung off the shutters in grey tongues; on the top step, Sam's hand stopped an inch from the doorbell.
It was a dark and stormy night when we arrived at the creepy old house.
questions.explanation: C selects precise details, replaces vague labels and shows fear through the paused hand — a literal 'zoom in'. A and B stack empty modifiers; D relies on cliché.
